claims.claim: Celeste Conowitch: 'keep it simple with a few powerful details' — the facts plus one detail ('reeks of garlic') that gives the room a story; never name the monster in narration.
claims.source: Kobold Press — Run your best actual play: Paint Me a Picture (Celeste Conowitch, 2026-07-20)
claims.quote: keep it simple with a few powerful details

claims.claim: Alexander's room formula: list notable things with positions, tag them with three of the five senses ('Try to include three of them'), then add a verb; NPCs get an action, clothing and one trait — 'you're not describing their headshot'.
claims.source: The Alexandrian — Random GM Tip: Description Formulas (2022-02-08)
claims.quote: Try to include three of them

claims.claim: Anne K. Brown's essay (as reported): use all five senses and show rather than tell ('you detect orcs' is the failure), but don't over-invest in sensory prose players can't use.
claims.source: Gaming Ballistic — Ballistic's Report: How to Write Adventure Modules that Don't Suck (2017-07-19)
claims.page: report on Brown, 'Listen! Do You Smell Something?'

claims.claim: Chris Doyle's essay (as reported): write read-aloud like a newspaper lead — immediate threat first ('GIANT SLAVERING OGRE'), secondary details after, lower-level details left for searching.
claims.source: Gaming Ballistic — Ballistic's Report: How to Write Adventure Modules that Don't Suck (2017-07-19)
claims.page: report on Doyle, 'How to Write Encounters that Don't Suck'

claims.claim: Sly Flourish: use fantastical language — 'quit writing read-aloud text that sounds like it came from Ikea instructions' — and make sure 'every word has a place in it'.
claims.source: Sly Flourish — Writing Awesome Read-Aloud Text (Mike Shea, 2010-11-08)
claims.quote: sounds like it came from Ikea instructions

claims.feature: punchy, emotionally slanted commercial boxed text
claims.claim: A review of dScryb's commercial boxed text finds it 'very punchy and to the point', carrying 'emotional information, motivations, or default assumptions' and sometimes 'selling' the creature or place.
claims.quote: very punchy and to the point

claims.feature: active voice and expletive cuts (editor via critic)
claims.claim: Vallese's book, per Lynch: cut 'there is/are' openings ('An old wise man watches over the children'), prefer active constructions, and reorder stacked modifiers ('Its wormlike body is thin and scaly').
claims.source: tenfootpole.org — Writing with Style: An Editor's Advice for RPG Writers review (Bryce Lynch, 2018-08-13)
claims.quote: Its wormlike body is thin and scaly

claims.claim: Vallese: 'Do you have to follow all of these tips all the time? Nope… Just be sure you understand the rules before you break them' — vary to keep flavor and voice.
claims.source: Gnome Stew — Review: Writing with Style (J.T. Evans, 2017-10-23)
claims.quote: Just be sure you understand the rules before you break them

claims.claim: Laws' fifth key: use plurals to dodge gendered pronouns — 'Characters can leave their pistols at the door.'
claims.source: Pelgrane Press — Five Keys to Punchier Prose (Robin D. Laws, 2012-02-01)
claims.quote: Characters can leave their pistols at the door

claims.claim: BAATAG rule 7: replace 'to be' verbs with active ones and show rather than tell — describe details that reveal information through play.
claims.source: Being An Asshole To A Goblin — Elements of a Key 4: Rules for Key-Writing (Misha F, 2026-04-28)

claims.claim: Merwin prefers the term 'narrative text': 'a series of prompts that can help your game flow more smoothly'; 'Excellent boxed text does a lot of heavy lifting' for atmosphere.
claims.source: D&D Sage Advice (sageadvice.eu) — 'This is exactly why boxed text is important' (Shawn Merwin, 2021-11)
claims.quote: Excellent boxed text does a lot of heavy lifting

claims.claim: Merwin (2019): 'A majority of DMs out there WANT boxed text (well-written hopefully)' — omitting it is 'a risk', even though streamers rarely read it.
claims.source: D&D Sage Advice (sageadvice.eu) — 'What are your thoughts on boxed text?' (Shawn Merwin tweet, 2019-04-14)
claims.quote: A majority of DMs out there WANT boxed text

claims.claim: Alexander rejects 3e's Traps/Creatures/Tactics/Development/Treasure key format because writers 'fill the format' and information lands out of play sequence: the ogre in the middle comes first, the goblin behind the tapestry does not.
claims.source: The Alexandrian — The Art of the Key (2014)

claims.claim: The essential key: room title, boxed text ('seen in a glance'), reactive checks front-loaded, bold-titled significant elements, developing details from general to specific, a GM-background tag — and 'Complete sentences are overrated'.
claims.source: The Alexandrian — The Art of the Key, Part 2: The Essential Key (2014-05-21)

claims.claim: Designing Dungeons: first paragraph describes 'everything immediately observable' with interactables in bold; list contents in the order described; monsters go last in the first description but first in later keying.
claims.source: Designing Dungeons — Chapter 10: Formatting Room Descriptions (Josh McCrowell & Warren D)
claims.quote: Write a paragraph that describes everything immediately observable

verdicts.trueWording: keep it simple with a few powerful details
verdicts.note: Kobold Press page (Celeste Conowitch, July 20, 2026) carries the quote word for word. Every limb holds: 'give the players the facts they need, and one thing to get them invested'; 'You step into a small stone room that reeks of garlic' -- 'the room has a story, a quirk'; and on naming monsters, 'describing the troll without ever using the word troll. It drives me bonkers when GMs use monster names.'

verdicts.trueWording: Try to include three of them in each description
verdicts.note: The Alexandrian (Feb 8, 2022) verbatim. Room formula: 'List every notable thing in the room and its position'; 'Use the Three of Five rule' with the parenthetical 'Think about your five senses. Try to include three of them in each description.'; 'If appropriate, add a verb.' NPC formula reads 'An action. What are they wearing? One physical trait.' and closes 'you're not describing their headshot, you're establishing them in the scene.'

verdicts.trueWording: five senses acting in dynamic concert; 'you detect orcs'
verdicts.note: Claim carried an empty quote field, but its one embedded quotation, 'you detect orcs', is on the page word for word, and every limb is supported. Gaming Ballistic (July 19, 2017) reports: "Listen! Do You Smell Something? By Anne K. Brown hits on some really good tips... available for consumption by the five senses acting in dynamic concert"; 'show, don't tell'; 'a much more subtle way to convey information than "you detect orcs."'; and 'She covers overdoing it too... if your players can't or won't use the information, it can be cut.' Caveat worth carrying forward: the 'you detect orcs' contrast is the reviewer's own illustration inside his report of Brown's essay, which the claim's '(as reported)' framing does cover.

verdicts.trueWording: GIANT SLAVERING OGRE is moving through broken furniture
verdicts.note: The quotation is on the page verbatim, twice, and the ordering limbs all hold -- immediate threat first, 'the rest can be dealt with after the party has survived the immediate threat', 'use newspaper conventions - big details that are right in your face up front, and details later', and 'the more your party searches, the more paragraphs can be read.' What fails is the attribution. The reviewer introduces the whole newspaper-lead passage as HIS addition to Doyle: 'One thing that might be implied but could be made explicit' -- an explicit disclaimer that Doyle's essay does not say it -- and then credits the advice to someone else: 'In fact, Juan Ochoa gave me that advice about giving him art direction.' What the page does attribute to Doyle is the encounter checklist (read-aloud text, description and details, stats, how a critter fights, treasure, consequences and developments) and the balance line 'first, it goes without saying that encounters need to be balanced for the adventuring party.'
verdicts.unsupportedLimb: that the newspaper-lead ordering is Chris Doyle's -- the page flags it as the reviewer's own addition ('might be implied but could be made explicit') and credits it to Juan Ochoa

verdicts.trueWording: quit writing read-aloud text that sounds like it came from Ikea instructions
verdicts.note: Sly Flourish (Mike, 8 November 2010) verbatim under the heading 'Keep it fantastic': 'We're playing a fantasy roleplaying game, quit writing read-aloud text that sounds like it came from Ikea instructions.' The second quoted fragment is verbatim too, under 'Keep it short': 'Ensure every word has a place in it.'

verdicts.trueWording: The descriptions themselves are very punchy and to the point
verdicts.note: Gnome Stew, Jared Rascher, July 27th 2021. All three quoted fragments verbatim: 'The descriptions themselves are very punchy and to the point'; monster descriptions 'often convey emotional information, motivations, or default assumptions about the creature'; and 'Some descriptions are slanted towards "selling" the creature or location being described to trigger an emotional effect.' The claim says 'creature or place' where the page says 'creature or location' -- outside its quotation marks, so not a verbatim failure.

verdicts.trueWording: After: Its wormlike body is thin and scaly
verdicts.note: tenfootpole.org, Bryce Lynch, August 13 2018, reviewing Ray Vallese. Stacked-modifier example verbatim: 'Before: Its body is thin, scaly, and wormlike. After: Its wormlike body is thin and scaly.' Expletive constructions verbatim: filler phrases 'there is' and 'there are'; 'There is an old wise man who watches over the children.' converted to 'An old wise man watches over the children.' The active-voice limb is supported more loosely -- the page lists 'Future vs Present Tense, my old friend passive voice, and a host of other examples' among what Vallese addresses, rather than stating an active-voice rule outright.

verdicts.trueWording: Just be sure you understand the rules before you break them
verdicts.note: Gnome Stew, J.T. Evans, October 23rd 2017, quoting page four of Vallese: 'Do you have to follow all of these tips all the time? Nope. It's fine to break them to add variety to your writing. In fact, you should. Don't hammer all the flavor or voice out of your text to rigidly adhere to guidelines. Just be sure you understand the rules before you break them.' The claim's ellipsis elides exactly that flavor/voice sentence, which is also the limb it asserts.

verdicts.trueWording: Characters can leave their pistols at the door, or leave them on the ship
verdicts.note: Pelgrane Press, By Robin D. Laws, posted February 1, 2012. Verbatim: 'The character can leave his pistol at the door, or leave it on the ship. Becomes: Characters can leave their pistols at the door, or leave them on the ship.' The 'fifth key' limb checks out by counting the article's five sub-headings: Passive Voice, Weak Verbs, Paring 'of the', Deprecation of the 'will', and Plurals Are Pluralistic -- the plurals section is fifth and last. Rationale verbatim: 'turn the subject plural to avoiding assuming gender for your hypothetical subject.'

verdicts.trueWording: check for 'to be' verbs and replace them with something more active
verdicts.note: No quotation was supplied to check word for word, so this grades as substance, but the page supports every limb of Rule 7 directly. BAATAG (Misha F, April 2026), 'Rule 7: Information should be presented in the manner in which the players can discover it... This is "show, don't tell", but even more so... A rote way to help with this is to check for usage of "to be" verbs and replace them with something more active. This can be as simple as replacing "there is a painting of the king" with "the painting reveals the form of the king", but it's a good check to make sure that you're describing information that can actually be revealed in play.' The author's own retrospective later on the page reinforces it: he 'completely avoid[ed] statements of being in favor of statements of action (Rule 7)'.

verdicts.trueWording: Excellent boxed text does a lot of heavy lifting
verdicts.note: sageadvice.eu reproduces two Shawn Merwin tweets. November 23, 2021: 'It's more than description. It's a series of prompts that can help your game flow more smoothly.' November 26, 2021: '(Perhaps that's why I prefer to call it "narrative text"). Excellent boxed text does a lot of heavy lifting, and atmosphere is definitely part of that burden.' Both quoted fragments verbatim, the preference for 'narrative text' explicit, and the atmosphere limb explicit. The host post itself is dated May 24, 2022; the tweets it archives are the 2021-11 ones the claim cites.

verdicts.trueWording: A majority of DMs out there WANT boxed text (well-written hopefully)
verdicts.note: sageadvice.eu archives the Shawn Merwin tweet of April 14, 2019 verbatim: '...A majority of DMs out there WANT boxed text (well-written hopefully) to make their lives easier when they buy adventure content. So it is a risk not to provide what your audience and consumers want.' The streaming limb is in the same block: 'if boxed text worked well, then we would see it used on the streams as a go-to to start a scene. I don't think we ever see it.' Note that streaming sentence is the point Merwin is replying to ('A point I was trying to make was...' then 'While this is true...'), not a separate source. Host post dated May 5, 2019.

verdicts.trueWording: tends to encourage writers to 'fill the format'
verdicts.note: The Alexandrian, May 19th 2014. The format named is confirmed as 3rd Edition's: 'When 3rd Edition arrived... First appearing in The Sunless Citadel, this format had the familiar boxed text and wall of text, but supplemented this with a specific set of bold-faced sections: Traps Creatures Tactics Development Treasure' -- exactly the five the claim lists, in order. Quote verbatim, and the ogre/goblin illustration verbatim: 'A room with an ogre standing in the middle of it should talk about the ogre first; a room with a goblin hiding behind a tapestry, on the other hand, shouldn't lead off with the goblin.' Plus 'the rigid adventure format forces information to be presented out-of-sequence.'

verdicts.trueWording: Complete sentences are overrated: Get the information across efficiently
verdicts.note: The Alexandrian, Part 2, May 21st 2014. Every component is a section heading or explicit line on the page: 'TITLE OF THE ROOM'; 'BOXED TEXT... I also think of this section as seen in a glance'; 'REACTIVE SKILL CHECKS -- Directly after the boxed text are the reactive skill checks which should be made immediately'; 'SIGNIFICANT ELEMENTS... Notice that the bold title makes it easy to find the information you need'; 'DEVELOPING SIGNIFICANT ELEMENTS... move from the general to the specific'; 'GM BACKGROUND TAG'. Closing line verbatim: 'Complete sentences are overrated: Get the information across in the most efficient fashion possible.'

verdicts.trueWording: Write a paragraph that describes everything immediately observable
verdicts.note: dungeons.hismajestytheworm.games Chapter 10: Formatting Room Descriptions. Quote verbatim, continuing 'by adventurers first entering the room... In this paragraph, highlight anything that's interactable in bold.' Ordering limb verbatim under 'First described, first keyed': 'Your bullet points should follow the same order as they were listed in the description.' Monster limb verbatim under 'Except monsters': 'I list obvious dangers like monsters last in my introductory paragraphs. However, because I know that players will want to interact with those elements first, I list those monsters first in subsequent keying.' One note: the page carries no byline, so the 'Josh McCrowell & Warren D' authorship in the source field is not confirmable from this page -- it is not a limb of the claim sentence, which the page supports in full.
